unit: Unit 2: AS 10 Property, Plant and Equipment
note: AI-written summary of ICAI study material. Check the original for exact wording.

topics.title: Objectives, Scope and Exceptions of AS 10 (Revised)
explain: AS 10 (Revised) prescribes the accounting treatment for Property, Plant and Equipment (PPE).
It helps financial statement users understand an entity's investment in PPE and changes in such investments.
Primary accounting issues include recognition of PPE, determining carrying amounts, depreciation, and impairment losses.
AS 10 applies to all PPE except when another standard permits different treatment (e.g., AS 19 for lease recognition).
It does NOT apply to biological assets (other than bearer plants) related to agricultural activity.
It does NOT apply to wasting assets like mineral rights, oil, natural gas, and non-regenerative resources.

flow.title: Scope Applicability Test under AS 10
steps: Check if asset is tangible item
Check if used for production or admin
Exclude non-bearer biological assets
Exclude wasting assets and mineral rights
Apply AS 10 to valid PPE

topics.example: A dairy farm owns milk-processing machinery and cows. The machinery is covered by AS 10 (Revised), whereas cows (living animals) are excluded until a specific Agriculture standard is issued.
remember: Bearer plants ARE covered by AS 10 (Revised), but produce growing on bearer plants is NOT.
Investment properties must be accounted for using ONLY the Cost Model under AS 10.
mistakes: Assuming AS 10 applies to the apples growing on an apple tree (produce is excluded; only the bearer tree is included).

quiz.q: Which of the following items is EXCLUDED from the scope of AS 10 (Revised)?
o: Bearer plants used to produce tea leaves
Machinery used in a manufacturing plant
Mineral rights and oil extraction reserves
Office equipment used for administrative work
quiz.why: Wasting assets, mineral rights, and extraction of oil and natural gas are specifically excluded from AS 10.

quiz.q: How must Investment Property (as defined under AS 13) be accounted for under AS 10 (Revised)?
o: Using Fair Value Model only
Using Cost Model only
Using Revaluation Model only
At Net Realisable Value
quiz.why: Clarification 2 states that investment property should be accounted for only using the Cost Model prescribed in AS 10.

topics.title: Definition of PPE & Bearer Plants
explain: PPE are tangible items held for use in production/supply of goods or services, rental to others, or administrative purposes.
They are expected to be used for more than 12 months.
Intangible items are covered separately under AS 26.
Administrative purposes includes selling, distribution, finance, accounting, personnel, and general business functions.
Safety and environmental equipment qualify as PPE because they enable an entity to derive economic benefits from related assets.
A Bearer Plant is a living plant used in production of agricultural produce, expected to bear produce for > 12 months, with remote likelihood of being sold as produce (except scrap).

flow.title: Two-Condition PPE Criteria
steps: Is the item tangible?
Held for production, rental, or admin?
Expected useful life > 12 months?
Both conditions met?
Classify item as PPE

topics.example: A rubber tree yields latex for 20 years and its scrap wood is eventually sold as firewood. The tree is a Bearer Plant (PPE), but annual crops like wheat are not.
remember: Safety equipment qualifies as PPE even if it does not directly increase future economic benefits on its own.
Incidental scrap sales of old bearer plants do not prevent them from being classified as bearer plants.
mistakes: Treating annual crops like maize or wheat as Bearer Plants.

quiz.q: Which of the following satisfies the definition of a Bearer Plant under AS 10 (Revised)?
o: Trees grown exclusively for timber/lumber
Annual crops like wheat and maize
Tea bushes cultivated to produce tea leaves for 15 years
Plants cultivated to be harvested as agricultural produce
quiz.why: Tea bushes meet all 3 conditions: used in production of produce, expected to bear for >12 months, and low likelihood of being sold as produce.

quiz.q: Why do safety and environmental assets qualify as PPE?
o: Because they directly generate cash inflows on their own
Because they enable an enterprise to derive future benefits from related assets
Because they have no acquisition cost
Because they are intangible assets under AS 26
quiz.why: Without safety or environmental assets, the entity cannot operate related assets to derive economic benefits.

topics.title: Initial Recognition & Elements of Cost
explain: PPE cost is recognized as an asset if future economic benefits are probable and cost can be measured reliably.
Cost includes purchase price, import duties, and non-refundable purchase taxes, minus trade discounts and rebates.
Cost includes directly attributable expenses to bring the asset to its required location and operating condition.
Directly attributable costs include employee benefits, site preparation, initial delivery, installation, testing, and professional fees.
Net proceeds from selling items produced while testing (e.g., test samples) are deducted from cost.
Cost includes initial estimate of decommissioning, dismantling, and site restoration obligations.
Costs of inauguration, advertising, staff training, and general admin overheads are EXCLUDED and expensed.

flow.title: Determining Cost of Purchased PPE
steps: Start with Purchase Price
Add non-refundable taxes and import duties
Deduct trade discounts and rebates
Add directly attributable installation/site costs
Add present value of dismantling obligation
Deduct net test-run sale proceeds
Final Initial Cost of PPE

topics.example: A company buys machinery for ₹1,58,00,000, pays ₹1,40,000 for site preparation, ₹1,35,00,0 technician salary for setup, ₹50,000 transport, and ₹30,000 architect fees. Total capitalized cost = ₹1,61,55,000.
remember: Capitalization STOPS when the asset is in the location and condition intended by management.
Initial operating losses and relocation costs CANNOT be capitalized.
mistakes: Capitalizing staff training costs or inauguration event costs into plant cost.

quiz.q: Which of the following costs CANNOT be capitalized as part of PPE?
o: Site preparation costs
Professional fees for installation
Costs of staff training for a new facility
Initial delivery and handling charges
quiz.why: Staff training and new location setup costs are specifically excluded from PPE cost and expensed.

quiz.q: How are net proceeds from selling sample items produced during testing of a machine treated?
o: Recognized directly as revenue in P/L
Deducted from the cost of testing before capitalization
Added to the purchase price of the machine
Credited to revaluation reserve
quiz.why: Testing costs are capitalized after deducting net proceeds from selling items produced while bringing the asset to location/condition.

topics.title: Self-Constructed Assets & Exchange of Assets
explain: Self-constructed asset costs follow the same principles as acquired assets; internal profits are eliminated.
Abnormal amounts of wasted material, labor, or other resources are NOT included in asset cost.
Borrowing costs are capitalized if criteria in AS 16 are satisfied.
Incidental revenues not necessary for construction (e.g., car park income from vacant site) go to P/L, not asset cost.
Acquisition of PPE in exchange for non-monetary asset is measured at FAIR VALUE of asset given up.
If fair value of asset received is more clearly evident, use that instead.
If exchange lacks commercial substance or fair value cannot be measured, measure at WDV (carrying amount) of asset given up.

flow.title: Measurement of Asset Acquired in Exchange
steps: Check if exchange has commercial substance
If NO commercial substance, record at WDV
If YES, check if Fair Value is measurable
Measure at Fair Value of asset given up
If received asset FV is clearer, use that
Recognize gain or loss in P/L

topics.example: Entity A exchanges land (WDV ₹10,00,000) for cash ₹20,00,000 + plant valued at ₹25,00,000. Total fair value received = ₹45,00,000. Gain of ₹35,00,000 is recognized in P/L.
remember: A transaction has commercial substance if cash flow configurations or entity-specific values change significantly.
If an exchange lacks commercial substance, NO profit or loss is recognized on the exchange.
mistakes: Recording an exchange lacking commercial substance at fair value instead of carrying amount (WDV).

quiz.q: When an entity acquires PPE by exchanging a non-monetary asset in a transaction that LACKS commercial substance, how is the acquired asset measured?
o: At its fair market value
At the carrying amount (WDV) of the asset given up
At liquidation value
At discounted present cash flow value
quiz.why: If an exchange transaction lacks commercial substance, the acquired asset is measured at the WDV of the asset given up.

quiz.q: What is the accounting treatment for abnormal waste during self-construction of a factory building?
o: Capitalized as part of the building cost
Added to borrowing costs under AS 16
Expensed immediately and excluded from building cost
Credited to revaluation reserve
quiz.why: Abnormal amounts of wasted material or labor are not included in the cost of self-constructed assets.

topics.title: Subsequent Costs & Component Accounting
explain: Day-to-day servicing, repairs, and maintenance are expensed in P/L when incurred.
Replacement parts (e.g., furnace relining, aircraft seats) are capitalized if recognition criteria are met.
When a replacement part is capitalized, the carrying amount of the replaced old part is derecognized.
Regular major inspections (e.g., aircraft overhaul) are capitalized as a replacement if criteria are met.
Any remaining carrying amount of previous major inspection cost is derecognized.
Component Depreciation: Each significant part of PPE with a cost significant to total cost must be depreciated separately.
If WDV of old part isn't known, use current replacement cost discounted back as an estimate of original cost.

flow.title: Subsequent Expenditure Decision Tree
steps: Is expenditure day-to-day repair/maintenance?
If YES, expense to P/L
If NO, is it part replacement or inspection?
Does it meet PPE recognition criteria?
Capitalize new cost to asset WDV
Derecognize WDV of old replaced part

topics.example: An airline replaces aircraft engines every 6 years. Engine cost is capitalized, and the carrying value of old engines is removed from books.
remember: Derecognition of replaced old parts occurs even if the old part's cost was not separately identified initially.
Parts with similar useful lives and depreciation methods may be grouped for component accounting.
mistakes: Capitalizing routine daily repairs instead of charging them to Profit & Loss.

quiz.q: Under AS 10 (Revised), how should routine day-to-day repairs and maintenance of machinery be accounted for?
o: Capitalized into the cost of machinery
Recognized as an expense in Statement of Profit and Loss
Debited to Revaluation Surplus
Deferred over 5 years
quiz.why: Costs of day-to-day servicing are repairs and maintenance, expensed in P/L as incurred.

quiz.q: When a major inspection cost is capitalized into the carrying amount of an aircraft, what happens to the carrying amount of the previous inspection?
o: It continues to be depreciated alongside the new cost
It is derecognized immediately
It is added to revaluation reserve
It is transferred to inventory
quiz.why: Any remaining carrying amount of the cost of the previous inspection is derecognized.

topics.title: Cost Model vs Revaluation Model
explain: An entity must choose either Cost Model or Revaluation Model as its accounting policy for an ENTIRE class of PPE.
Cost Model: PPE is carried at Cost minus Accumulated Depreciation minus Accumulated Impairment losses.
Revaluation Model: PPE is carried at Revalued Amount (Fair value at revaluation date minus subsequent accumulated depreciation/impairment).
Revaluations must be done with sufficient regularity so carrying amount does not differ materially from fair value.
If an item of PPE is revalued, the ENTIRE class of PPE to which it belongs must be revalued.
Initial revaluation increase is credited directly to Revaluation Surplus (Owners' Interest).
Revaluation increase reversing a previous decrease charged to P/L is recognized in P/L to the extent of that decrease.
Initial revaluation decrease is charged to P/L; decrease reversing existing surplus is debited to Revaluation Surplus.

flow.title: Accounting for Revaluation Increase / Decrease
steps: Determine Revaluation outcome
If Upward: check for prior P/L decrease
Credit P/L up to prior decrease, balance to Surplus
If Downward: check for prior Revaluation Surplus
Debit Surplus up to existing balance, balance to P/L

topics.example: Land cost ₹1,00,000. Revalued to ₹1,50,000 in Year 2 → ₹50,000 credited to Revaluation Reserve. In Year 4, fair value drops to ₹1,30,000 → ₹20,000 debited to Revaluation Reserve.
remember: Transfers from Revaluation Surplus to Revenue Reserves on disposal are NOT made through P/L.
Volatile assets need ANNUAL revaluation; stable assets can be revalued every 3 to 5 years.
mistakes: Revaluing only one office building while keeping other office buildings in the same class at historical cost.

quiz.q: An asset costing ₹1,00,000 was revalued DOWN to ₹90,000 in Year 2 (₹10,000 charged to P/L). In Year 4, it is revalued UP to ₹1,05,000. How is the ₹15,000 increase treated?
o: Entire ₹15,000 credited to Revaluation Reserve
₹10,000 credited to P/L and ₹5,000 credited to Revaluation Reserve
Entire ₹15,000 credited to P/L
₹15,000 debited to P/L
quiz.why: Revaluation increase reverses previous P/L decrease of ₹10,000 in P/L, and the remaining ₹5,000 is credited to Revaluation Reserve.

quiz.q: If an entity chooses to revalue its factory buildings, what must it do regarding other factory buildings in the company?
o: Keep other factory buildings at historical cost
Revalue the entire class of factory buildings
Revalue only half of the factory buildings
Depreciate remaining buildings to zero
quiz.why: If an item of PPE is revalued, the entire class of PPE to which that asset belongs must be revalued.

topics.title: Depreciation Accounting & Useful Life
explain: Depreciable Amount = Cost (or revalued amount) minus Residual Value.
Depreciation is systematically allocated over the asset's useful life.
Useful life is the period an asset is expected to be available for use OR the output units expected from it.
Factors determining useful life: expected usage, physical wear & tear, technical/commercial obsolescence, legal limits.
Residual value and useful life must be reviewed at least at EACH financial year-end.
Changes in useful life or residual value are treated as changes in accounting estimates under AS 5 (applied PROSPECTIVELY).
Depreciation BEGINS when the asset is AVAILABLE FOR USE (ready in position and condition intended by management).
Depreciation DOES NOT CEASE when asset becomes idle or retired from active use unless fully depreciated.
Methods: Straight-line (constant charge), Diminishing Balance (decreasing charge), Units of Production (based on output).
Revenue-based depreciation method is NOT PERMITTED.

flow.title: Life & Depreciation Review Process
steps: Review useful life and residual value annually
Compare with previous estimates
Calculate remaining unamortized WDV
Divide unamortized WDV over new remaining life
Apply prospectively as AS 5 estimate change

topics.example: Asset bought for ₹1,00,000 (10 yr life). At end of Year 4, WDV = ₹60,000. Remaining life revised to 4 years. New annual depreciation = ₹60,000 / 4 = ₹15,000 per year.
remember: Land has unlimited life and is NOT depreciated (except quarries/landfill sites).
Depreciation starts when asset is ready for use, NOT when commercial production actually starts.
mistakes: Using revenue generated by an asset as the basis for calculating depreciation (prohibited).

quiz.q: When does depreciation of an asset COMMENCE under AS 10 (Revised)?
o: On the date actual commercial production begins
When the asset is ready and available for use as intended by management
At the end of the financial year
When the asset is fully paid for
quiz.why: Depreciation begins when the asset is available for use (in the location and condition intended by management).

quiz.q: Which of the following depreciation methods is NOT PERMITTED under AS 10 (Revised)?
o: Straight-line method
Diminishing balance method
Revenue-based depreciation method
Units of production method
quiz.why: A depreciation method based on revenue generated by an activity is not appropriate/permitted under AS 10.

topics.title: Decommissioning Changes & Impairment Compensation
explain: Subsequent changes in decommissioning/restoration liabilities alter asset cost depending on measurement model used.
Under Cost Model: Changes in liability are added to or deducted from asset cost in current period.
Deduction cannot exceed asset carrying amount; any excess reduction is recognized immediately in P/L.
Under Revaluation Model: Liability decrease credits Revaluation Surplus (or reverses prior P/L deficit).
Under Revaluation Model: Liability increase is charged to P/L (or debited to Revaluation Surplus up to credit balance).
If asset reaches end of useful life, subsequent changes in liability are recognized in P/L immediately.
Compensation from third parties for impaired/lost PPE is included in P/L when it becomes RECEIVABLE.

flow.title: Decommissioning Liability Adjustment under Cost Model
steps: Estimate change in decommissioning liability
If INCREASE: add to asset cost
Check if asset needs impairment test
If DECREASE: deduct from asset cost
If deduction exceeds WDV, write off excess to P/L

topics.example: A machine destroyed in fire had WDV ₹2,00,000. Insurance company replaces it with new machine worth ₹20,00,000. Entity records loss of ₹2,00,000 on old machine derecognition and gain/receivable of ₹20,00,000 when insurance claim is virtually certain.
remember: Third-party impairment compensation and new replacement asset purchases are TWO SEPARATE economic events.
Insurance claim income is recognized only when receipt is virtually certain under AS 29.
mistakes: Offsetting insurance claim compensation against the carrying value of destroyed old asset directly.

quiz.q: Under the Cost Model, if a decrease in decommissioning liability exceeds the carrying amount of the asset, how is the excess treated?
o: Added to revaluation reserve
Recognized immediately in Statement of Profit and Loss
Deducted from future years' depreciation
Carried as negative asset value
quiz.why: If a decrease in liability exceeds carrying amount, the excess is recognized immediately in P/L.

quiz.q: How should an entity account for insurance compensation received for a destroyed PPE item?
o: Adjust directly against original cost of destroyed asset
Include in P/L when compensation becomes receivable as a separate transaction
Credit to revaluation surplus
Ignore until new asset is purchased
quiz.why: Compensation from third parties for impaired/lost PPE is included in P/L when it becomes receivable.

topics.title: Retirement, Derecognition & Disclosures
explain: PPE retired from active use and held for disposal is stated at lower of Carrying Amount and Net Realizable Value (NRV).
Any write-down to NRV is recognized immediately in P/L.
Derecognition: Carrying amount of PPE is derecognized on disposal (sale, finance lease, donation) OR when no future economic benefits are expected.
Gain or Loss on derecognition = Net Disposal Proceeds minus Carrying Amount, recognized in P/L.
Gains on disposal CANNOT be classified as revenue under AS 9.
Disclosures required: Measurement bases, depreciation methods, useful lives/rates, gross carrying amount & accumulated depreciation, reconciliation of carrying amount.
Additional disclosures: Restrictions on title, pledged assets, construction expenditures, contractual commitments.
Revalued assets disclosures: Effective date, independent valuer involvement, methods/assumptions, revaluation surplus.

flow.title: Derecognition & Gain/Loss Calculation
steps: Identify disposal event or end of benefits
Determine Net Disposal Proceeds
Determine Carrying Amount at disposal date
Calculate Gain or Loss
Recognize Gain or Loss in P/L
Remove asset WDV from financial statements

topics.example: A machine with WDV ₹1,87,50,000 is sold for ₹1,12,50,000. Loss on disposal of ₹75,00,000 is charged to P/L, and ₹1,00,00,000 revaluation reserve is transferred to Retained Earnings.
remember: Revaluation surplus on derecognized asset is transferred directly to Retained Earnings, NOT through P/L.
PPE held for routine rental and then sold in ordinary business is transferred to Inventory at WDV before sale.
mistakes: Classifying gain on sale of factory machinery as Revenue from Operations under AS 9.

quiz.q: Items of PPE retired from active use and held for disposal should be carried at:
o: Historical cost
Revalued amount
Lower of Carrying Amount and Net Realisable Value
Fair value plus selling costs
quiz.why: Retired assets held for disposal are stated at the lower of carrying amount and net realisable value.

quiz.q: When a revalued asset is sold, how is its remaining Revaluation Surplus balance transferred?
o: To Statement of Profit and Loss as income
Directly to Revenue Reserves / Retained Earnings
To Deferred Tax Liability
To Capital Redemption Reserve
quiz.why: The revaluation surplus included in owners' interest may be transferred directly to Revenue Reserves / Retained Earnings when derecognized.
